claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schuppler et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of actomyosin in the Drosophila embryo ectoderm resulted in the edges of an activated square becoming concave as the square contracted.
claims.source: Remarkably, optogenetic activation of actomyosin in the complex environment of the Drosophila embryo ectoderm had a similar effect: the edges of an activated square became concave as the square contracted (Izquierdo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Izquierdo et al., 2018.

claims.claim: In simulations, an activated circle of myosin nodes displayed isotropic contraction.
claims.source: Not surprisingly, an activated circle displayed isotropic contraction (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In simulations, the sides of an activated solid square of myosin nodes became concave.
claims.source: Notably, the sides of an activated solid square became concave (Figure 1C), mimicking both the in vitro (Schuppler et al., 2016) and in vivo studies (Izquierdo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1C and matches in vitro and in vivo observations.

claims.claim: In simulations, the outer sides of a hollow square with a thin boundary of activation became convex.
claims.source: The outer sides of a hollow square with a thin boundary of activation became convex (Figure 1D), mimicking the in vitro behavior (Schuppler et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1D and matches in vitro observations.

claims.claim: For a hollow square with a thick boundary of activation, the outer sides of the boundary became concave and the inner edges bent in the opposite direction in simulations.
claims.source: For a hollow square with a thick boundary of activation, the outer sides of the boundary became concave and the inner edges bent in the opposite direction (Figure 1E), as also seen in vitro (Schuppler et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1E and matches in vitro observations.

claims.claim: When simulated individually, a centrally induced Arp2/3 network grows centrifugally with an outer perimeter of non-aligned actin plus end nodes.
claims.source: When simulated individually, a centrally induced Arp2/3 network grows centrifugally with an outer perimeter of non-aligned actin plus end nodes (Figure 1G), a behavior resembling initial in vivo growth of an actin cap in the embryo surface plane (e.g. Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1G and compared to in vivo observations.

claims.claim: Arp2/3 network growth against a cantilever leads to an increased density of F-actin plus ends at the interface, without an accumulation of elastic energy in vitro.
claims.source: By combining light and atomic force microscopy, Bieling et al., 2016 found that Arp2/3 network growth against a cantilever lead to an increased density of F-actin plus ends at the interface, without an accumulation of elastic energy (Bieling et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bieling et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In simulations, with Arp2/3 network growth into an immovable wall, the density of plus end nodes within 20 pixels of the network circumference increased 1.57-fold from the start of the simulation to step 3000.
claims.source: With network growth into the immovable wall, the density of plus end nodes within 20 pixels of the network circumference increased 1.57-fold from the start of the simulation to step 3000 (calculated from four simulations with distinct starting conditions; see images in Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from simulation data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: For simulated Arp2/3 networks growing without a wall, the density of plus end nodes within 20 pixels of the network circumference decreased 0.77-fold by simulation step 3000.
claims.source: For networks growing without a wall, the equivalent value decreased 0.77-fold by simulation step 3000 (see example images in Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from simulation data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: In simulations, network area growth rates after removal of the wall were indistinguishable from those of networks that never experienced a wall.
claims.source: However, network area growth rates after removal of the wall were indistinguishable from those of networks that never experienced a wall (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: In simulations, a broad ring of myosin nodes with zero myosin activity maintained its structure.
claims.source: Without myosin activity (0.0), the broad ring maintained its structure (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: In simulations, with full myosin activity (1.0), a broad ring of dispersed nodes initially constricted into a narrow ring of nodes, and after thinning, the ring constricted centripetally.
claims.source: With full myosin activity (1.0), the broad ring of dispersed nodes initially constricted into a narrow ring of nodes, and after thinning, the ring constricted centripetally (Figure 2E), a sequence of events consistent with in vitro observations of a myosin network activated in a rectangular shape (Schuppler et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2E and compared to in vitro observations.

claims.claim: In simulations, adding a growing Arp2/3 network to the center of a broad ring with zero or moderate myosin activity led to centrifugal displacement of myosin nodes and a thinning of the ring, but no ring constriction was observed.
claims.source: Adding a growing Arp2/3 network to the center of a broad ring with zero or moderate myosin activity led to centrifugal displacement of myosin nodes and a thinning of the ring, but no ring constriction was observed (Figure 2B,D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claims.claim: In simulations, as the Arp2/3 network grew, the thinned ring of myosin nodes was displaced outward and displayed diminished circularity that resembled the rough outer edge of the segregated Arp2/3 network.
claims.source: As the Arp2/3 network grew, the thinned ring of myosin nodes was displaced outward and displayed diminished circularity that resembled the rough outer edge of the segregated Arp2/3 network.
claims.evidence: This is observed in simulation data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claims.claim: In simulations, during displacement by Arp2/3 network growth, the two networks remained segregated and myosin nodes aggregated at the network-network interface.
claims.source: During this displacement, the two networks remained segregated, confirming the effectiveness of the node-based rules, and myosin nodes aggregated at the network-network interface (Figure 2B,D, arrows).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claims.claim: In simulations, with full myosin node activity, the actomyosin ring counteracted the expansion of the central Arp2/3 network.
claims.source: With full myosin node activity, the actomyosin ring counteracted the expansion of the central Arp2/3 network (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: In control RNAi embryos during the transition from mitotic cycle 10 to 11, the actomyosin network initially assembled a rough, non-circular interface around each myosin-devoid cap, but within minutes, smooth and circular boundaries formed.
claims.source: In control RNAi embryos during the transition from mitotic cycle 10 to 11, the actomyosin network initially assembled a rough, non-circular interface around each myosin-devoid cap, but within minutes, smooth and circular boundaries formed (Figure 3A; the transition was most obvious for completely new networks formed between sister nuclei, solid black arrows).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In Arp3 RNAi embryos, actomyosin networks failed to form smooth boundaries and instead retained a variable distribution of puncta at the interface with the myosin-devoid cap.
claims.source: In contrast, Arp3 RNAi embryos assembled actomyosin networks that failed to form smooth boundaries and instead retained a variable distribution of puncta at the interface with the myosin-devoid cap (Figure 3A, solid red arrows).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In control embryos, the formation of a smooth interface was often accompanied by an accumulation of Zip-GFP along the interface.
claims.source: In control embryos, the formation of a smooth interface was often accompanied by an accumulation of Zip-GFP along the interface (Figure 3A, solid and hollow black arrows), and both demarked the site of initial pseudo-cleavage furrow ingression (Figure 3A, 143s, side view, blue arrowheads).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Arp3 RNAi embryos lacked Zip-GFP accumulation at the interface and furrow ingression failed.
claims.source: Arp3 RNAi embryos lacked Zip-GFP accumulation at the interface (Figure 3A, solid and hollow red arrows) and furrow ingression failed (Figure 3A, 143s, side view, blue bracket shows a broad band of myosin at the embryo surface).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The Arp2/3-based actin network of the cap is required for forming a smooth interface with the actomyosin border.
claims.source: These data suggest that the Arp2/3-based actin network of the cap is required for forming a smooth interface with the actomyosin border, and that smooth interface formation coincides with myosin accumulation and furrow initiation at the interface.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A comparing control and Arp3 RNAi embryos.

claims.claim: Smooth interface formation coincides with myosin accumulation and furrow initiation at the interface.
claims.source: These data suggest that the Arp2/3-based actin network of the cap is required for forming a smooth interface with the actomyosin border, and that smooth interface formation coincides with myosin accumulation and furrow initiation at the interface.
claims.evidence: This is observed in in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Both actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks initially have a rough boundary.
claims.source: Notably, both networks initially have a rough boundary (Zhang et al., 2018; Figure 3A), and the smooth interface seems to arise from their lateral interaction.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018 and in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The smooth interface seems to arise from the lateral interaction of the actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks.
claims.source: Notably, both networks initially have a rough boundary (Zhang et al., 2018; Figure 3A), and the smooth interface seems to arise from their lateral interaction.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A and simulation results.

claims.claim: In simulations without Arp2/3 networks, at node densities that retained connectivity (0.1–0.25), higher myosin activities (0.2–1.0) produced smooth and circular boundaries with the clearances.
claims.source: At node densities that retained connectivity (0.1–0.25), higher myosin activities (0.2–1.0) produced smooth and circular boundaries with the clearances (Figure 3C, yellow arrows).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: High myosin activity is sufficient to produce extended, smooth structures in vivo, such as cell junction-associated actomyosin cables or the cytokinetic ring.
claims.source: This result is consistent with the sufficiency of myosin activity to produce extended, smooth structures in vivo, such as cell junction-associated actomyosin cables (Harris, 2018; Livne and Geiger, 2016) or the cytokinetic ring (Schwayer et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harris, 2018; Livne and Geiger, 2016; and Schwayer et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In simulations without Arp2/3 networks, low myosin activity (0.1) allowed persistence of rough boundaries with the clearances.
claims.source: In contrast, low myosin activity (0.1) allowed persistence of rough boundaries with the clearances (Figure 3C; red arrows), and displayed modest network rearrangements during early stages of the simulation (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claims.claim: The simulated myosin distribution with low activity and rough boundaries resembled the myosin distribution in Arp3 RNAi embryos.
claims.source: This result resembled the myosin distribution in Arp3 RNAi embryos (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is concluded by comparing simulation data in Figure 3C-D with in vivo data in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Myosin activity is relatively low in the early Drosophila embryo.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that myosin activity is relatively low in the early embryo.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from simulation results and in vivo observations, and supported by citations to studies showing inhibitors of myosin activity are required for maintaining proper syncytial architecture.

claims.claim: Several inhibitors of myosin activity are required for maintaining proper syncytial architecture of the early Drosophila embryo.
claims.source: Indeed, several inhibitors of myosin activity are required for maintaining proper syncytial architecture of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), and a specific mechanism locally elevates myosin activity for budding and full division of mono-nucleated primordial germ cells from the syncytium (Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; and Zhang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: A specific mechanism locally elevates myosin activity for budding and full division of mono-nucleated primordial germ cells from the syncytium.
claims.source: Indeed, several inhibitors of myosin activity are required for maintaining proper syncytial architecture of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), and a specific mechanism locally elevates myosin activity for budding and full division of mono-nucleated primordial germ cells from the syncytium (Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013.

claims.claim: In simulations, centrifugal cap growth with weakly contractile actomyosin networks (0.1 activity) resulted in improved local smoothness but the network-network interface was wavy, and each clearance gained a hexagon-like shape.
claims.source: Compared with the myosin network boundaries formed in the absence of Arp2/3 networks (Figure 3C–D), local smoothness improved but the network-network interface was wavy, and each clearance gained a hexagon-like shape (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Sensitivity analyses showed a failure to form a smooth and circular interface over a wide range of parameter values affecting the myosin network, the Arp2/3 network, and their interface.
claims.source: Sensitivity analyses showed a failure to form a smooth and circular interface over a wide range of parameter values affecting the myosin network, the Arp2/3 network, and their interface (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by sensitivity analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6.

claims.claim: In simulations, Arp2/3 network growth induced an aggregation of myosin nodes at the interface.
claims.source: However, Arp2/3 network growth did induce an aggregation of myosin nodes at the interface (Figure 4A, arrows).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In simulations, myosin node connections became substantially longer than their resting length specifically at the interface, and only with Arp2/3 network growth.
claims.source: Also, myosin node connections became substantially longer than their resting length specifically at the interface, and only with Arp2/3 network growth (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In the presence of growing Arp2/3 networks, node-node connections of two or more pixels greater than resting length rose linearly from 0% of all connections at simulation step 0, to 0.48 ± 0.01% at step 500, to 2.05 ± 0.06% at step 2500.
claims.source: In the presence of growing Arp2/3 networks, node-node connections of two or more pixels greater than resting length rose linearly from 0% of all connections at simulation step 0, to 0.48 ± 0.01% at step 500, to 2.05 ± 0.06% at step 2500 (calculated from four simulations with distinct starting distributions, a myosin node density of 0.2, and a myosin node activity of 0.1; p<0.001 comparing steps 500 and 2500).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from simulation data with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In the absence of growing caps, the percentages of stretched connections remained at <0.003% from simulation steps 0 to 2500.
claims.source: In the absence of growing caps, the percentages remained at <0.003% from simulation steps 0 to 2500.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from simulation data.

claims.claim: Arp2/3 network growth aggregated myosin nodes at the interface and increased tension between myosin nodes at the interface.
claims.source: Thus, Arp2/3 network growth aggregated myosin nodes at the interface and increased tension between myosin nodes at the interface.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: In vivo imaging revealed an Arp2/3-dependent accumulation of myosin at the smooth and circular interface between each cap and myosin border.
claims.source: Although proper syncytial structure requires regulators that reduce cortical actomyosin activity (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), our in vivo imaging revealed an Arp2/3-dependent accumulation of myosin at the smooth and circular interface between each cap and myosin border (Figure 3A, black arrows).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity is evident in vivo.
claims.source: Mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity is evident in vivo (Effler et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009), and implicated mechanisms include stabilization of the myosin-actin interaction (Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; Yamashiro et al., 2018), and alignment of actin filaments for optimal myosin activity (Ennomani et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Effler et al., 2006 and Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Implicated mechanisms for mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity include stabilization of the myosin-actin interaction.
claims.source: Mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity is evident in vivo (Effler et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009), and implicated mechanisms include stabilization of the myosin-actin interaction (Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; Yamashiro et al., 2018), and alignment of actin filaments for optimal myosin activity (Ennomani et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; and Yamashiro et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Implicated mechanisms for mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity include alignment of actin filaments for optimal myosin activity.
claims.source: Mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity is evident in vivo (Effler et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009), and implicated mechanisms include stabilization of the myosin-actin interaction (Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; Yamashiro et al., 2018), and alignment of actin filaments for optimal myosin activity (Ennomani et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ennomani et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In simulations, myosin node activity elevation events occurred predominantly at interfaces between the actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks.
claims.source: However, comparison of myosin node activity elevation events with and without Arp2/3 networks revealed that the elevations occurred predominantly at interfaces between the actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks (Figure 4C, arrows), and that they required the Arp2/3 network (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Arp2/3-dependent activations of interface myosin in silico resembled the Arp2/3-dependent accumulations of interface myosin in vivo.
claims.source: These Arp2/3-dependent activations of interface myosin in silico resembled the Arp2/3-dependent accumulations of interface myosin in vivo (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is concluded by comparing simulation data in Figure 4C with in vivo data in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In simulations, mechanosensitive myosin node activity elevations significantly enhanced the smoothness and circularity of the interfaces.
claims.source: Strikingly, the elevations significantly enhanced the smoothness and circularity of the interfaces (Figure 4D), compared to simulations without the elevations (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4D compared to Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Quantifications of clearance smoothness, circularity, and area showed the importance of a combination of Arp2/3 network growth and mechanosensitivity of the actomyosin network.
claims.source: Quantifications of clearance smoothness, circularity, and area showed the importance of a combination of Arp2/3 network growth and mechanosensitivity of the actomyosin network (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Sensitivity analyses showed that the smooth and circular interfaces arose upon inclusion of mechanosensitivity over a wide range of parameter values affecting the myosin network, the Arp2/3 network, and their interface.
claims.source: Sensitivity analyses showed that the smooth and circular interfaces arose upon inclusion of mechanosensitivity over a wide range of parameter values affecting the myosin network, the Arp2/3 network, and their interface (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by sensitivity analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6.

claims.claim: The overall organization of the myosin networks simulated with mechanosensitivity and Arp2/3 network growth closely resembled the myosin networks formed in the presence of Arp2/3 actin caps in wild-type embryos.
claims.source: The overall organization of the myosin networks simulated with mechanosensitivity and Arp2/3 network growth (Figure 4D) closely resembled the myosin networks formed in the presence of Arp2/3 actin caps in wild-type embryos (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is concluded by comparing simulation data in Figure 4D with in vivo data in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: A smooth and circular interface can form from the growth of an Arp2/3 network against a weakly contractile actomyosin network that is mechanosensitive to local activation.
claims.source: These analyses suggest that a smooth and circular interface can form from the growth of an Arp2/3 network against a weakly contractile actomyosin network that is mechanosensitive to local activation.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: In simulations of an isolated single ring of myosin nodes with uniform activity, the inner boundary nodes initially moved centrifugally as the ring thinned, and then moved centripetally as the thin and smooth ring constricted.
claims.source: Figure 5A traces the movements of myosin nodes at the inner boundary of the rough ring. Consistent with our single ring analyses in Figure 2E, the inner boundary nodes initially moved centrifugally as the ring thinned (Figure 5A), and then moved centripetally as the thin and smooth ring constricted (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In simulations of an isolated single ring, at the beginning of the simulation, a broad distribution of node displacement angles was observed.
claims.source: At the beginning of the simulation, a broad distribution of node displacement angles was observed (Figure 5C), but during the transition from thinning to constricting, the distribution became biased toward 0° and 180° relative to local radii of the circular network (Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In simulations of an isolated single ring, during the transition from thinning to constricting, the distribution of node displacement angles became biased toward 0° and 180° relative to local radii of the circular network.
claims.source: At the beginning of the simulation, a broad distribution of node displacement angles was observed (Figure 5C), but during the transition from thinning to constricting, the distribution became biased toward 0° and 180° relative to local radii of the circular network (Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claims.claim: In simulations of an isolated single ring, nodes mostly displayed back-and-forth displacements closely aligned with the radii during the final stages of the simulation.
claims.source: To understand this bimodal distribution, we examined individual node displacements at full temporal and spatial resolution during the final stages of the simulation. Strikingly, nodes mostly displayed back-and-forth displacements closely aligned with the radii (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The oriented oscillations of nodes provided a signature of contractile actomyosin ring formation in simulations.
claims.source: Although the in vivo relevance of these extremely rapid oscillations is unclear, the oriented oscillations provided a signature of contractile actomyosin ring formation in our simulations.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In two-network simulations, Arp2/3 network growth displaced the myosin nodes centrifugally throughout the simulation, including stages of elevated myosin node activity and when the network-network interface became smooth and circular.
claims.source: Arp2/3 network growth displaced the myosin nodes centrifugally throughout the simulation, including stages of elevated myosin node activity and when the network-network interface became smooth and circular (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: In two-network simulations, initially, a broad distribution of local displacement angles occurred for activated myosin nodes.
claims.source: Initially, a broad distribution of local displacement angles occurred (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: In two-network simulations, the phase of smoothening and circularization was accompanied by a bimodal distribution dominated by angles near 0° and 180° for activated myosin nodes.
claims.source: In contrast, the phase of smoothening and circularization was accompanied by a bimodal distribution dominated by angles near 0° and 180° (Figure 5I–J).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5I-J.

claims.claim: The mechanical elevation of myosin node activity by the pushing forces of Arp2/3 network growth produces a contractile actomyosin ring around the network-network interface.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that the mechanical elevation of myosin node activity by the pushing forces of Arp2/3 network growth produces a contractile actomyosin ring around the network-network interface, and that contractility of this ring smoothens and circularizes the interface.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Contractility of the actomyosin ring smoothens and circularizes the interface.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that the mechanical elevation of myosin node activity by the pushing forces of Arp2/3 network growth produces a contractile actomyosin ring around the network-network interface, and that contractility of this ring smoothens and circularizes the interface.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks have been individually simulated as continuum or agent-based models.
claims.source: Actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks have been individually simulated as continuum or agent-based models (Berro, 2018; Cortes et al., 2018; Mogilner and Manhart, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berro, 2018; Cortes et al., 2018; and Mogilner and Manhart, 2016.

claims.claim: The investigation of roughly distributed elements rearranging into a smooth structure required an agent-based approach.
claims.source: Our investigation of roughly distributed elements rearranging into a smooth structure required an agent-based approach.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice based on the research question.

claims.claim: The formation of an extended, smooth interface across a 2D plane is not trivial.
claims.source: The formation of an extended, smooth interface across a 2D plane is not trivial.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Tensile forces can align polymers, but the two ends of the network must be anchored.
claims.source: Tensile forces can align polymers, but the two ends of the network must be anchored.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a general principle based on physical understanding.

claims.claim: A network can anchor to itself, as in the case of a cytokinetic ring.
claims.source: Since a network can anchor to itself, as in the case of a cytokinetic ring (Schwayer et al., 2016), intra-network anchorage may explain the formation of smooth boundaries within a multiply fenestrated myosin network with high contractility (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwayer et al., 2016 and simulation data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Low contractility networks cannot form smooth boundaries on their own.
claims.source: However, low contractility networks cannot form smooth boundaries on their own.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claims.claim: Low contractility is important for maintaining the syncytial state of the early Drosophila embryo.
claims.source: Low contractility is important for maintaining the syncytial state of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), arrays of podosomes at the base of invasive mammalian cells (Rafiq et al., 2017), and the polar body bud during meiosis II arrest of mouse oocytes (Yi and Li, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; and Zhang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Low contractility is important for arrays of podosomes at the base of invasive mammalian cells.
claims.source: Low contractility is important for maintaining the syncytial state of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), arrays of podosomes at the base of invasive mammalian cells (Rafiq et al., 2017), and the polar body bud during meiosis II arrest of mouse oocytes (Yi and Li, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rafiq et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Low contractility is important for the polar body bud during meiosis II arrest of mouse oocytes.
claims.source: Low contractility is important for maintaining the syncytial state of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), arrays of podosomes at the base of invasive mammalian cells (Rafiq et al., 2017), and the polar body bud during meiosis II arrest of mouse oocytes (Yi and Li, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yi and Li, 2012.

claims.claim: Disruptive effects of widespread contractility can be avoided by the local induction of contractility in one material in response to pushing forces from a neighboring material.
claims.source: Our simulations indicate that disruptive effects of widespread contractility can be avoided by the local induction of contractility in one material in response to pushing forces from a neighboring material, and that this induction can produce a contractile ring to smoothen the interface between such materials.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: In the Drosophila embryo, the smooth and circular interface demarcates where the plasma membrane folds to form a dome-like compartment.
claims.source: In the Drosophila embryo, the smooth and circular interface demarcates where the plasma membrane folds to form a dome-like compartment.
claims.evidence: This is stated based on in vivo observations shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Without sufficient growth of the actin cap, the interface remains rough and membrane folding fails.
claims.source: Without sufficient growth of the actin cap, the interface remains rough and membrane folding fails (Figure 3A; Stevenson et al., 2002; Zallen et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 3A and citations to Stevenson et al., 2002 and Zallen et al., 2002.

claims.claim: With weakening of the myosin border, the actin cap grows with an irregular shape and the plasma membrane invagination is lop-sided around the cap.
claims.source: With weakening of the myosin border, the actin cap grows with an irregular shape and the plasma membrane invagination is lop-sided around the cap (Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The simulations show how a smooth and circular structure can emerge from the local interactions of roughly distributed components.
claims.source: Our simulations of network-network interactions at the surface of the early Drosophila embryo show how a smooth and circular structure can emerge from the local interactions of roughly distributed components.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from all simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: This example of refinement by mechanical self-organization is relevant to other cell biological processes, such as mammalian polar body budding and podosome protrusion.
claims.source: This example of refinement by mechanical self-organization is relevant to other cell biological processes, such as mammalian polar body budding (Yi and Li, 2012) and podosome protrusion (van den Dries et al., 2019).

results.result: The simulated actomyosin network mimics mesoscale properties of actomyosin networks reconstituted in vitro. Specifically, activated circles contract isotropically, solid squares develop concave edges, thin hollow squares develop convex outer edges, and thick hollow squares show concave outer edges with oppositely bent inner edges.
results.evaluation: Claims C26 and C32-C35 demonstrate that the simulation reproduces in vitro behaviors reported by Schuppler et al., 2016 and in vivo behaviors by Izquierdo et al., 2018. The simulation data in Figure 1B-E directly matches the cited experimental observations, validating the actomyosin network model.

results.result: The simulated Arp2/3 network mimics properties of Arp2/3 networks reconstituted in vitro. When growing against a wall, plus end node density increases at the interface without accumulating elastic energy, matching in vitro observations by Bieling et al., 2016.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 show that the Arp2/3 simulation reproduces key in vitro behaviors: centrifugal growth with non-aligned plus ends (C36), increased plus end density at interfaces with obstacles (C37-C39), and lack of elastic energy accumulation (C40). The quantitative measurements from simulations (1.57-fold increase with wall, 0.77-fold decrease without) support the model's validity.

results.result: The network-network interface simulation maintains segregation and allows mutual displacement. Without myosin activity, rings maintain structure; with full activity, rings constrict. Adding Arp2/3 networks causes centrifugal displacement and myosin node aggregation at interfaces, with the two networks remaining segregated.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 demonstrate that the interface rules work as intended. The simulations show appropriate responses to varying myosin activity (C42-C43), proper network segregation during Arp2/3 growth (C44-C46), and mutual force balance (C47). Figure 2 provides clear visual and quantitative evidence supporting these behaviors.

results.result: In vivo, Arp2/3 is required for forming smooth and circular boundaries between actin caps and actomyosin borders in Drosophila embryos. Arp3 RNAi embryos fail to form smooth boundaries, lack myosin accumulation at interfaces, and show failed furrow ingression.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C48-C53 are strongly supported by in vivo imaging data in Figure 3A showing the rough-to-smooth transition in control embryos and persistent rough boundaries in Arp3 RNAi embryos. The correlation between smooth interface formation, myosin accumulation, and furrow initiation provides converging evidence for Arp2/3's requirement.

results.result: In simulations without Arp2/3 networks, low myosin activity (0.1) results in persistent rough boundaries, mimicking Arp3 RNAi embryos, while high myosin activity (0.2-1.0) produces smooth boundaries. This suggests myosin activity is relatively low in early Drosophila embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C56-C61 are well-supported by simulation data in Figure 3C-D showing the activity-dependent boundary formation. The resemblance between low-activity simulations and Arp3 RNAi phenotypes (C59) is compelling, and the inference about low in vivo myosin activity (C60-C61) is supported by cited literature on myosin inhibitors.

results.result: Adding expanding Arp2/3 networks to weakly contractile actomyosin networks (0.1 activity) results in wavy, non-circular interfaces despite myosin node aggregation and increased tension at the interface. Sensitivity analyses confirm this failure across a wide parameter range.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C63-C69 are supported by simulation data in Figure 4A-B and supplementary figures showing hexagonal clearances, myosin node accumulation, and quantified increases in stretched connections (0.48±0.01% at step 500 to 2.05±0.06% at step 2500, p<0.001). The extensive sensitivity analyses strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Incorporating mechanosensitive myosin activation into simulations allows Arp2/3 network growth to locally induce a contractile actomyosin ring that smoothens and circularizes the interface. This mechanism is evident both in silico and in vivo, with myosin accumulation at smooth interfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C70-C80 are strongly supported by simulation data (Figure 4C-E) showing interface-localized myosin activations and resulting smooth boundaries, matching in vivo observations (Figure 3A). Quantifications in Figure 4E demonstrate significant improvements in smoothness, circularity, and area. Sensitivity analyses (Figure 4 supplements 1-6) confirm robustness across parameter ranges.

results.result: Analysis of node movements reveals that mechanosensitive myosin activation by Arp2/3 network growth produces a contractile actomyosin ring. Nodes display back-and-forth oscillations aligned with local radii, providing a signature of ring formation that smoothens and circularizes the interface.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C90 are supported by detailed node tracking analyses in Figure 5 showing the transition from broad to bimodal angular distributions (0° and 180° relative to radii) in both single-ring and two-network simulations. The oscillatory behavior and its correlation with interface smoothening provide mechanistic insight, though the authors appropriately note uncertainty about in vivo relevance of rapid oscillations.

results.result: The simulations demonstrate that disruptive effects of widespread contractility can be avoided by local induction of contractility in response to pushing forces from a neighboring material. In Drosophila embryos, the smooth interface demarcates membrane folding sites, and disruption of either network component causes morphological defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 synthesize the main findings, supported by the complete simulation dataset and in vivo observations. The mechanistic explanation (C100) is well-supported by Figures 4-5, and the functional consequences (C101-C103) are supported by Figure 3A and cited literature (Stevenson et al., 2002; Zallen et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2018).

results.result: Background claims about cytoskeletal polymer properties: microtubules have high rigidity for transport, individual actin polymers have lower rigidity, but cross-linking can bundle actin into straight structures supporting protrusions.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 are standard textbook knowledge supported by appropriate citations (Hawkins et al., 2010; Salbreux et al., 2012; Svitkina, 2018). These provide context for the study but are not novel findings.

results.result: Background examples of mechanical self-organization in biological systems: wing disc compartment boundaries require myosin, mesenchymal migration involves follower cell smoothening, and cytokinesis involves myosin-dependent ring smoothening.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 cite established literature (Harris, 2018; Wang and Dahmann, 2020; Livne and Geiger, 2016; van Helvert et al., 2018; Schwayer et al., 2016) to provide biological context. These are accurate representations of prior work.

results.result: Background on cell cortex structure: it is a thin sheet-like material underlying the plasma membrane, composed of distinct formin-induced and Arp2/3-induced actin networks, with cortical asymmetry capable of eliciting flow and filament alignment.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14 accurately summarize established knowledge about cortex structure and properties, supported by appropriate citations (Chugh and Paluch, 2018; Svitkina, 2020; Munro, 2006; Reymann et al., 2016).

results.result: Background on polar body budding: involves an Arp2/3-enriched domain surrounded by a smooth actomyosin ring, with the Arp2/3 domain preventing full ring contraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 accurately cite Yi and Li, 2012 to provide biological context for similar network interactions in a different system.

results.result: Background on Drosophila embryo cortical organization: centrosomes induce Arp2/3-enriched caps surrounded by actomyosin borders, which initially have rough boundaries but form smooth interfaces. Network assembly is induced by small G proteins, and networks physically restrict each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C25 accurately summarize prior work on Drosophila embryo cortical organization, supported by multiple citations (Foe et al., 2000; Raff and Glover, 1989; Stevenson et al., 2001-2002; Zallen et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2018; Blake-Hedges and Megraw, 2019; Lv et al., 2021; Royou et al., 2004). These provide essential biological context.

results.result: Prior in vitro and in vivo studies show that actomyosin network reshaping is influenced by initial activation patterns: circles contract isotropically, solid squares develop concave edges, and hollow square outlines develop convex edges.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 accurately cite Schuppler et al., 2016 (in vitro) and Izquierdo et al., 2018 (in vivo) to establish the experimental basis for validating the simulation model.

results.result: Background on mechanosensitive actomyosin activation: mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity occurs in vivo through mechanisms including myosin-actin interaction stabilization and actin filament alignment.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 cite appropriate literature (Effler et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; Yamashiro et al., 2018; Ennomani et al., 2016) to justify the mechanosensitivity mechanism incorporated into the model.

results.result: Methodological justification: actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks have been simulated previously, but investigating rough-to-smooth transitions required an agent-based approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 appropriately cite prior modeling work (Berro, 2018; Cortes et al., 2018; Mogilner and Manhart, 2016) and justify the methodological choice based on the research question.

results.result: Discussion of smoothening mechanisms: forming smooth interfaces in 2D is non-trivial, tensile forces require anchorage, and low contractility is important in various biological contexts including Drosophila embryos, podosomes, and polar body budding.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 synthesize general principles and cite appropriate literature (Schwayer et al., 2016; Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Rafiq et al., 2017; Yi and Li, 2012) to contextualize the findings.

results.result: Discussion of broader implications: the mechanism is relevant to other biological processes (polar body budding, podosome protrusion) and to advanced manufacturing with smart materials, nanocomposites, and metamaterials.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 make speculative connections to other systems and applications. While C105 cites relevant biological examples (Yi and Li, 2012; van den Dries et al., 2019), claims C106-C109 about materials science applications are largely speculative despite citations (Begley et al., 2019; Holmes, 2019; Eder et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Galland et al., 2013). The relevance requires experimental validation.

results.result: Model parameters are based on biological measurements: cortex thickness (50-400 nm), myosin mini-filament properties (28-58 motor domains at angles up to 180°), optimal actin filament length (~500 nm), Arp2/3 branching angle (70°), and network mechanical properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C119 cite appropriate literature to justify model parameters (Chugh and Paluch, 2018; Salbreux et al., 2012; Svitkina, 2020; Billington et al., 2013; Niederman and Pollard, 1975; Laplante et al., 2016; Sellers and Kachar, 1990; Chugh et al., 2017; Banerjee et al., 2020; Pollard, 2016; Amann and Pollard, 2001; Pollard and Borisy, 2003). These provide essential methodological details.

results.result: Both actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks initially have rough boundaries, and the smooth interface arises from their lateral interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by in vivo imaging (Figure 3A) and cited literature (Zhang et al., 2018). This observation motivates the mechanistic investigation but is itself a relatively straightforward observation.

results.result: A specific mechanism locally elevates myosin activity for primordial germ cell budding and division from the syncytium.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 cites Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013 to provide context about regulated myosin activity in a specific developmental process. This is accurate background information.
